idiom_name: typed ES modules: export/import with import type, barrel index as the published surface
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits ES modules and adds types: a file with a top-level import or export is a module, the published surface is what is exported (values and types), and everything else is file-private, with import type and export type making type-only edges explicit so they are erased from the emitted JavaScript. A domain module is a directory exported through an index.ts barrel plus a tsconfig path alias (for example @billing/*), which keeps consumer imports on the published path; the legacy namespace keyword predates ES modules and is not recommended for new code because it does not participate in the file-level module graph. How the module is emitted (ESM or CommonJS) is a compiler decision: module and moduleResolution should match the runtime, and verbatimModuleSyntax keeps written form and output aligned.
pitfalls: Types can leak internals: exporting a type implemented by an unexported class reveals structure, so publish structural types deliberately.
export * silently drops names when two modules export the same identifier, and a barrel that re-exports everything publishes internals while slowing builds.
Type-only edges that are not marked with import type or the type modifier can pull a module into the runtime graph, hiding an unwanted dependency until the compiler elision changes.
Path aliases hide the boundary in the specifier: @billing can resolve to billing/index.ts while sibling files in the same folder stay importable by relative path.
